title: An analytics approach to designing combination chemotherapy regimens for cancer
contribution: Builds the first database of published advanced gastric-cancer chemotherapy trials (414 trials, 495 arms), predicts trial survival and toxicity out of sample from earlier trials, and plugs the fitted models into a MIO with an exploration bonus to propose phase II regimens and into a ranking to select phase III regimens, evaluated against oncologists' historical choices with a simulation metric and a matching metric.
problem_entry: {AP+DA+IO} Phase II trials mostly test new combinations of known drugs, trials are costly and phase II populations unrepresentative; prediction rules, meta-regressions and preclinical models cannot propose or score unseen combinations; enter by predicting trial outcomes before the trial and optimizing the regimen choice (pp. 2-4).
key_idea: Hand-built trial-arm database -> regularized regressions for median OS and DLT share trained only on earlier trials -> MIO (1) maximizing predicted OS plus an exploration bonus Gamma*t_d^(-1/2) under a predicted-toxicity limit, at most three drugs, never-tested regimens; phase III picks by population-adjusted prediction instead of raw phase II results (pp. 5-15).
assumptions: Linear outcome models with error variance sigma^2/n_i (weights n_i/mean n); 20 demographic/study and 216 drug variables (72 drugs x binary, instantaneous and average dose); DLT definitions and the 0.5 threshold read from 20 phase I/II protocols; mean filling and imputation (Grade 4 blood toxicities imputed in 46.5% of arms); only performance status controls treatment selection; trastuzumab excluded; doses limited to observed values; one screener and one extractor (pp. 5-8, 13, 19).
proof_devices: MIO (1): binaries plus continuous doses, linear ridge predictors in objective and toxicity constraint, cardinality N = 3 (89.1% of the database), drug-class constraints, novelty constraint, observed-dose sets; linearization of (1d)-(1e) not shown (pp. 12-13)
Exploration bonus u_d = t_d^(-1/2) motivated by the standard deviation of a sample mean (footnote 11, p. 12)

DLT composite: five combination rules between the max rule (lower bound) and the sum rule (upper bound), ranked by correlation with reported total Grade 3/4 toxicity on 36 arms; grouped independent wins with 0.893 (pp. 19-20)
Linear vs quadratic imputation chosen by residual sum of squares (p. 19)
Simulation metric with 40 bootstrap ground-truth coefficient sets and outcome feedback; matching metric with 0/1/10/100 mismatch penalties (pp. 15-16; App. B, pp. 20-21)
experiments: Chronological testing after the first 98 arms (347 survival, 307 toxicity predictions); last four-year window: ridge OOS R2 0.56 (bootstrap 0.53 [0.50, 0.57]), RMSE 2.50 vs 3.75 for a running-mean baseline, lasso R2 0.58, toxicity AUC 0.83 (SVM 0.87); flagging 10%/20% of high-toxicity trials at 0.4%/1.9% false flags; 27 phase III arms from 1997: simulated median OS +2.8 to +4.7 months in all 360 runs, toxicity not significantly different; matching +2.3/+3.5/+3.9 months with +0.02/+0.05/+0.12 high-toxicity share; model regimens almost always three drugs (100%/98% vs 31%/37%); no MIO solver, version or run time reported (pp. 9-18, 20).
positioning: Against patient-level clinical prediction rules, meta-analysis and meta-regression (explanatory, few drug variables, randomized trials only, no out-of-sample test) and preclinical models (no patient outcomes), presented as a complement to the latter; three 'to our knowledge' firsts; knowledge gradient and Q-learning deferred to future work (pp. 3-4, 18).
writing: Aspiration paragraph plus bulleted firsts (p. 3); Table 1 maps each model to its evaluation technique (p. 4); a bias-direction paragraph after each surrogate metric with an asymmetric reading (pp. 15-16); hedged abstract, but 'without changing toxicity outcomes' (p. 2) against 'without major changes' and +0.12 at t = 0.5 (p. 17).
limits_future: Stated: no trial run; the simulation assumes the ridge structure and may score infeasible regimens; matching scores in other populations; new drugs cannot be predicted; HER2 subgroup excluded; next a single-arm trial, then an RCT, preclinical constraints and interaction terms, other diseases (pp. 4, 13, 15-18). Unstated: single-person screening and extraction, the formulation's three-drug signature left unchanged (pp. 5, 16-17).

method_links.note: owner = trial planners; baseline = regimens oncologists chose for 27 phase III experimental arms; decisions scored by simulated and matched outcomes, not prediction accuracy; limits of the evaluation stated; single-arm then randomized trial proposed (the step-6 instance the skill cites)
fitted linear predictors keep regimen design inside a MIO, but no solver, version or solve time is reported (the stop rule's measured solve time is missing)
no certificate or gap for model (1); the duel is with practitioners' historical choices and, for prediction, a running-mean baseline, not a warm-start heuristic
toxicity limit t and exploration weight Gamma swept on a 3x3 grid with a published table of survival gain and toxicity change; no knob-property bound; differences between settings within noise

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Surrogate evaluation with stated bias direction
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: simulation metric (model structure assumed true, may score infeasible regimens: bias in the model's favour) and matching metric (other populations: bias either way), read asymmetrically: favourable results merit a trial, unfavourable ones end the line

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Counterfactual replay against the historical decision-maker
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: history rerun from 1997: the model chooses where oncologists chose, simulated outcomes are fed back into training, both choices scored on the same ground truths; also in S143 (150-week replay, [card S143, p. 4]) and S079 (matched imputation, [card S079, p. 5])

transferable: Chronological out-of-sample testing for anything built from historical cases: sort by date, predict each case only from earlier ones, keep sibling records (other arms of the same trial) out, start after a burn-in share (p. 9).

When a decision cannot be field-tested yet, evaluate it with two surrogates whose biases run in different directions (a simulator over bootstrap-plausible ground truths; matching to the closest real future case), state each bias, and let only favourable results justify the next, costlier test (pp. 14-16; App. B, pp. 20-21).
Put an exploration bonus proportional to (prior tests)^(-1/2) of each component into the optimization objective, with one weight swept in the evaluation (pp. 12, 16).
Restrict continuous decisions to values observed in the data (doses used in some trial) so the optimizer cannot propose unprecedented quantities (constraint (1e), p. 13).
Read thresholds and composite definitions off the domain's own documents (DLT lists and the 0.5 cut-off from phase I protocols) instead of inventing them (pp. 6-7).

Bracket an aggregate that cannot be computed from marginals between a max rule (lower bound) and a sum rule (upper bound), and pick a rule in between by correlation on the cases that report the aggregate (pp. 19-20).
Report how the optimizer's decisions differ in kind from practice (regimen size, age of drugs, novelty share), not only in outcome (pp. 16-17).
coauthors: Allison O'Hair, Stephen Relyea, John Silberholz

title: OR forum—an algorithmic approach to linear regression
contribution: Builds linear regression models with one MIQO that imposes sparsity, group sparsity, limited pairwise collinearity, transform selection, expert-mandated variables and a robustifying l1 term jointly, enforces significance and conditioning by cutting off failing supports, and shows on synthetic and real data sparser, less collinear models at accuracy comparable to the Lasso.
problem_entry: {ML+IO} Regression is built by trial and error, one property at a time, and textbooks give no guidance on balancing the properties; the task fits MIQO but is not modelled so because of the intractability belief; enter by replacing the textbook 'standard approach' with one MIQO that also certifies infeasibility when properties conflict (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: MIQO (5): support indicators with big-M, cardinality k, constraint families for groups, correlated pairs, transforms and mandated variables, and Gamma*||beta||_1 as robustification (Theorem 1, cited: robust least squares equals regularized regression and recovers the Lasso); bootstrap significance and condition number enforced by no-good cuts on the top three supports; sweep k and Gamma, select by validation R2 (pp. 5-8).
assumptions: Linear model; norm-bounded uncertainty on X; bootstrap instead of distributional assumptions; pairwise correlation as multicollinearity surrogate plus condition number <= 30; fixed transform menu (x^2, sqrt x, log x); defaults rho = 0.8, ten Gamma values, three Stage-3 rounds, 50/25/25 split; big-M from data; synthetic Toeplitz Gaussian designs with k = 10; twelve public real sets plus four case studies (pp. 2-14).
proof_devices: Theorem 1 cited (Bertsimas-Fertis 2009; Xu et al. 2009): robust least squares equals a norm-regularized problem; p = 2, q = 1 recovers the Lasso (p. 6)
Big-M support linking -M z_l <= beta_l <= M z_l with M estimated from data (pp. 7-8)
Constraint families (5d)-(5h): cardinality, equal indicators for groups, z_i + z_j <= 1 for correlated pairs, at most one transform per variable, forced inclusion (pp. 7-8)
No-good cut sum over S_i of z_l <= |S_i| - 1 removing a failing support (Stage 3, p. 8)
k_max as the maximum stable set of the correlation-conflict graph, solved as a small MIO (p. 7)
Warm start by discrete first-order methods from the best-subset paper (p. 5)
Speed-up arithmetic: CPLEX 29,000 x Gurobi >27 = 780,000 solver factor times about 570,000 hardware factor = about 450 billion; MILO factors asserted similar for MIQO (p. 4)
experiments: Gurobi 6.0.0 / JuMP 0.7.0 / Julia 0.3.3 on a 16-core Xeon with 128 GB; 20 s (n>p) or 40 s (n<p) per MIQO, about 0.3-2.1 h per synthetic experiment; MIQO recovers the true support with 1-2 extras vs about 24/45 for the Lasso at similar R2, with half the maximum correlation; real data: fewer variables, but the Lasso has higher test R2 on 7 of 12 sets (Pyrimidines 0.367 vs 0.175, discussed; Diabetes 0.381 vs 0.334, not); Croq'Pain same model as the manual approach in under a minute; Ames 20 variables, R2 0.920; Concrete 0.823 with 6 variables vs Lasso 0.834 with 12; combined example: Lasso wins the noisiest cell (0.368 vs 0.245); Tables 3 and 7 carry identical entries with rows reversed except Time; no gaps reported (pp. 9-15).
positioning: Against the textbook standard approach (Chatterjee et al.), Furnival-Wilson (MIQO-based but accurate only for p <= 30), the Lasso (conditions unverifiable; accuracy credited to robustness), group Lasso, PCR/PLS and shrinkage, analytic post-selection inference; speed-up history from Bixby and Nemhauser; devices from the group's own papers (pp. 3-7).
writing: Abstract template practice -> belief -> 450 billion -> method (p. 2); 'astonishing' four times (pp. 2-4); an aspirations section dividing labour between humans and machines (p. 2); Table 1 maps properties to model lines (p. 3); teaching-case examples before the experiments (pp. 8-10); 'only methodology we are aware of' twice (pp. 3, 15); one-paragraph conclusion without limits (p. 15).
limits_future: No limits or future work stated (p. 15); visible: time-limited MIQOs on Diabetes and HIV (p. 11), hours of run time (pp. 11-12), lower R2 than the Lasso on most real sets (p. 13), the Table 3/7 duplication (p. 12), infeasibility certificate never exercised.

method_links.note: abstract leads with practice, belief and figure; belief dated to the 1970s-1980s and conceded as justified then; figure rebuilt from solver version tests (780,000) times Top500 hardware (570,000) = about 450 billion, the figure the skill dates to AoS 2016, here in a second paper

factors are for mixed-integer linear problems; the MIQO factor is asserted 'similar' without a source (the skill's checkpoint); the same hardware factor recurs in S011, where the total becomes 800 billion through the solver factor alone
a statistics-owned modelling process written as one MIQO that keeps its class
trial-and-error loop replaced by one MIQO; warm starts; stated limits, solver, machine and versions; duel with the Lasso tuned on the same validation set; synthetic known-truth plus real data
certificate promised (suboptimality and infeasibility) but no gaps reported, two real sets end at the time limit, infeasibility never demonstrated
'the price of insisting on interpretability' named, knob rho handed to the analyst with two points of the curve (Pyrimidines, Tables 9-10); no solution-independent bound
part of a named programme (2013 Morse lectureship, modern optimization lens) and a student's thesis line; examples are teaching cases (own Croq'Pain case, Ames class project)

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Lazy no-good cuts for properties checked outside the model
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: bootstrap significance and condition number are checked on the top three supports; failing supports are excluded with sum over S of z_l <= |S| - 1 and the MIQO is resolved, up to three rounds

transferable: Turn each rule of thumb of a modelling craft into a constraint on support indicators: equal indicators for groups, z_i + z_j <= 1 for conflicting pairs, sum of z <= 1 over a variable's transforms, z = 1 for expert-mandated variables (pp. 7-8).

For properties that can only be checked after fitting (bootstrap significance, condition number), check the best few incumbents, cut each failing support off with a no-good cut, resolve, and cap the rounds (p. 8).
Before sweeping a cardinality k, compute the largest feasible k as a maximum stable set on the conflict graph so that no infeasible MIQO is solved (p. 7).
Read the field's standard textbooks to define the current procedure step by step, then test against it on the textbooks' own teaching data sets (pp. 3, 8-10).
Report interpretability measures (K*, maximum pairwise correlation, condition number, true positives) beside test R2 so a sparser model's price is visible next to its gain (pp. 11-13).

quotes.text: Fitting regression models has long been viewed as an art
This is the price of insisting on interpretability

title: Inventory management in the era of big data
contribution: Applies conditional stochastic optimization with random-forest weights to the vendor-managed inventory of a major multimedia distributor, harvesting web covariates (IMDb, RottenTomatoes, Google Trends) and reporting a coefficient of prescriptiveness of 0.88 over a 150-week replay at 20,000 locations.
problem_entry: {DA+AP} Web data predict demand but those works stop short of optimal decisions under uncertainty; enter through a real vendor-managed inventory operation (about 1 billion units a year, more than 20,000 European retail locations) under shelf-capacity pressure (p. 1).
key_idea: Conditional stochastic optimization min_z E[c(z;Y)|X=x] with machine-learning weights (random forests) from the prescriptive-analytics preprint; decision problem: per location and week, maximize expected sell-through under shelf capacity, justified by scan-based trading; scored by the coefficient of prescriptiveness P (pp. 1-2, 4).
assumptions: Problem decomposes by week and location; X = recent item and location sales, chain, country, geocoded location, IMDb/RottenTomatoes title features, Google Trends attention at world, country and sub-national level; sales treated as censored demand and corrected by a Kaplan-Meier-type transform; properties of the method quoted from the earlier preprint (pp. 2-4).
proof_devices: Formulation (2): capacitated multi-item sell-through newsvendor max sum_j E[min{Y_j, z_j} | X = x] s.t. sum_j z_j <= K_r (p. 2)
Coefficient of prescriptiveness P as a unitless R2 for decisions, quoted from Bertsimas-Kallus 2014 (p. 2)
Asymptotic optimality and tractability quoted, not proved here (p. 2)
experiments: 150-week rolling replay (Dec 2011-Nov 2014), weekly retraining on past data only; comparators perfect foresight and SAA++ (no auxiliary data but product-age demand distributions); P = 0.88 averaged over 20,000 locations, three locations plotted; no absolute sell-through or cost, no spread across locations, no comparison with the vendor's current rule, no run times, deployment not stated (p. 4).
positioning: Against web-data demand prediction (Choi-Varian, Asur-Huberman, Da et al., Goel et al., Gruhl et al., Kallus 2014) that does not reach decisions; builds on Bertsimas-Kallus 2014; no inventory-theory references among the nine (pp. 1-2, 4).
writing: Award-feature genre: industry stakes first, the method's two properties as labelled paragraphs, one headline number repeated and translated into plain language; 'an 88% reduction in operational costs' (p. 2) looser than the definition as the share of the sell-through gap closed (p. 4); vendor anonymous; typos (pp. 1-4).
limits_future: No limits or future directions stated; absent are deployment status, the owner's current rule as baseline and absolute impact (p. 4).

method_links.note: owner (vendor), decision (weekly order quantities under capacity), auxiliary covariates rather than the uncertain demand itself, learning inside the decision (random-forest weights), decision metric P on sell-through, long out-of-sample replay; the data-poor baseline strengthened with product-age distributions (stronger naive rule in spirit)
baseline is a constructed policy (SAA++) and an oracle, not the vendor's current replenishment rule; no field test, no own costs reported

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Counterfactual replay against the historical decision-maker
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: rolling-origin weekly retraining and scoring over 150 weeks, each week using only prior data; also S078 (simulation and matching from 1997) and S079 (matched imputation)

transferable: Rolling-origin replay for a decision policy: at each period train only on the past, decide, then score on what happened; run it over years, not one split (p. 4).

Report a decision policy as the share of the gap it closes between a data-poor baseline (made as strong as fairness allows, e.g. age-dependent demand distributions) and the perfect-foresight bound (pp. 2, 4; note 3).

Turn public web traces into covariates aligned with the decision's geography and timing: sub-national search volume, title metadata, network communities of cast members, text clusters of plots (pp. 2-4).
Treat observed sales as censored demand and correct before learning (note 1, p. 4).

title: Optimal classification trees
contribution: Formulates CART's own tree-training problem exactly as a MIO (OCT) and, by relaxing split integrality, hyperplane trees (OCT-H); warm-started by CART and lower-depth solutions and solved by Gurobi 6.5 under time limits, they beat depth-matched CART by about 1-2% (OCT) and 3-5% (OCT-H) on 53 UCI data sets, mostly without certificates of optimality.
problem_entry: {ML+IO} Greedy top-down induction optimizes impurity split by split and needs pruning; Breiman et al. themselves called an overall optimal tree infeasible in 1984; earlier heuristics never certified optimality; enter by posing CART's own problem as a MIO now that MIO solvers are fast (pp. 4-6).
key_idea: OCT model (24): misclassification plus alpha*splits with leaf-size constraints over the maximal tree of depth D, solving exactly the problem CART approximates; OCT-H by relaxing split coefficients to [-1,1]^p with the same binaries; warm starts from trimmed CART and lower depths; alpha tuned through an integer split budget (pp. 9-19).
assumptions: Features scaled to [0,1]; K classes; N_min fixed at 5% of n; depths 1-4; synthetic Murthy-Salzberg ground-truth trees with label noise, feature noise, dimension and training size varied; 53 UCI data sets (n 47-5,456, p up to 484), 50/25/25 splits repeated five times; tens of thousands of points prohibitive (pp. 8, 20-26).
proof_devices: Maximal-tree indexing with left and right ancestor sets (p. 10)
Split switch d_t: a_t = 0, b_t = 0 sends all points right, so nodes can stop splitting without new variables (p. 11)
Strict inequality replaced by a per-feature epsilon_j (smallest nonzero gap between sorted values) with big-M constants from the scaling, M1 = 1 + epsilon_max, M2 = 1 (p. 12)
Leaf misclassification linearized with label indicators and M = n; loss normalized by baseline error so alpha does not depend on data-set size (p. 13)
Alpha tuning via integer split budget C = 1..C_max with warm-start chains in C and depth, dominated solutions removed, midpoint of the winning alpha interval (pp. 15-17)
OCT-H: |a_jt| linearized, M = 2, mu = 0.005 for the strict inequality, variable-use indicators s_jt penalized (pp. 17-18)
Speed-up arithmetic: Gurobi 1.0 -> 6.5 'nearly 50', solver total about 1.4 million, hardware about 570,000, about 800 billion (p. 6)
Difficulty set by the n*2^D binaries z_it; minutes for depth <= 4 and thousands of points (p. 14)
experiments: Gurobi 6.5 via JuMP/Julia on AWS c4.xlarge (4 vCPU, 7.5 GB), limits 30 min-2 h (OCT), 5-15 min (OCT-H); Wine depth 2: optimum found in 105 s and proved in 230 s more with CART warm start vs 270 s + 1,360 s without; synthetic: OCT closest to ground-truth structure, gains 1-2% at 15-20% label noise; real data mean accuracy depth 1-4: CART 71.0/76.2/78.8/79.8, OCT 71.3/78.0/79.5/80.4, OCT-H 76.1/81.0/82.3/82.9; OCT gains 0.36/1.86/0.73/0.62% (p-values given), OCT-H 5.12/4.88/3.59/3.12%; unconstrained CART 80.7% vs OCT depth-4 80.4%; random forests 85.8%; most results uncertified; CART baseline is trimmed rpart; 'when it wins' rules fitted on the same 53 sets (pp. 14-37).
positioning: CART defines the problem and Breiman is quoted twice; C4.5 choice called arbitrary (Murthy-Salzberg); lookahead, one-step 'optimal' and enumeration heuristics never certified; multivariate heuristics top-down; own CRIO judged plainly (no provable optimality, no significant gain); random forests used only to scale the gains (pp. 4-9, 36).
writing: Abstract template greedy practice -> 800 billion -> formulation -> headline numbers (p. 3); numbered contributions with numbers (pp. 6-7); strong verbs about beliefs ('refuting', 'widely-held belief', 'comprehensive evidence') with hedges in the body (pp. 3, 25-29, 37); headline gains rounded up against Tables 9-10 (pp. 7, 30-31, 37); random-forest comparison framed in advance (p. 36).
limits_future: Stated: tens of thousands of points prohibitive, most results uncertified, smaller gains at depths 3-4, N_min untuned, LR/SVM warm starts untested; future: tune N_min, a single tree as accurate as a random forest, longer limits for depth-4 OCT (pp. 19-20, 25-29, 37). Unstated: in-sample applicability rules; trimmed-CART baseline (pp. 25-26, 31-34).

method_links.note: abstract leads with greedy practice and the 800-billion figure; belief conceded in Breiman's 1984 words and as justified in the 1970s-1980s; figure rebuilt for this paper (Gurobi 6.5): against S081's 450 billion the hardware factor is unchanged and the whole increase comes from one solver release
the Gurobi 6.5 factor is referenced to Bixby 2012, Nemhauser 2013 and a 'Gurobi 6.0 performance benchmarks' PDF accessed September 2015, none of which by title and date covers version 6.5
the incumbent's own problem written exactly as a MIO, boundary printed (n*2^D binaries; minutes at depth <= 4; tens of thousands of points prohibitive)
one MIO replaces greedy splitting; CART is warm start and opponent; solver, machine, limits stated; matched-depth duel on 53 data sets; winning and losing regions printed

contradicts step 4: the paper argues a proof of optimality is not needed to evaluate a classifier and solves may stop when the incumbent stalls; most results carry no certificate while method and title say optimal (the skill's say-do caveat and Tension T1, confirmed at source)
doctoral student, programme brand and its paper series named

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Solve the incumbent heuristic's own objective exactly
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: OCT keeps CART's objective, parameters (alpha, N_min) and depth so that the comparison isolates exactness; depth-1 gains attributed to the objective change alone

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Relax the exact model to reach a richer class at no extra binaries
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: relaxing integrality of the split coefficients turns OCT into hyperplane trees with the same number of binaries and an easier solve
rules on CART accuracy, n/p and p predict when OCT or OCT-H beats CART, found by looking across all depths of the same 53 data sets (in sample)

transferable: Let a node switch off by zeroing its split (a_t = 0, b_t = 0 sends every point the same way), so tree size is decided inside the model without new variables (p. 11).
Replace a strict inequality by a data-derived margin, for each feature the smallest nonzero gap between sorted values, and read tight big-M constants off the feature scaling (p. 12).

Tune a continuous complexity penalty through its integer budget form, warm-starting each budget and depth from the previous one, discarding dominated solutions and taking the midpoint of the winning alpha interval (pp. 15-17).
Show upper- and lower-bound traces with and without the incumbent as warm start on one small instance, separating time to find from time to prove (Fig. 3, pp. 14-15).
Before real data, run a ground-truth recovery study (Murthy-Salzberg protocol) and report structure beside accuracy, varying training size, label noise, feature noise and dimension (pp. 20-25).
Decompose the gain: at depth 1 there is no global search, so a gain there measures the change of objective alone (p. 29).
Print per-data-set results with wins, losses, ties and p-values, the losses included (pp. 28-29, 37-45).

title: Personalized diabetes management using electronic medical records
contribution: Proposes a kNN-based prescriptive rule for type 2 diabetes regimens from Boston Medical Center records that switches a patient's regimen only when predicted HbA1c improves by at least 0.8%, and estimates retrospectively a mean HbA1c reduction of 0.14% over all visits and 0.44% where the algorithm departs from the standard of care.
problem_entry: {DA+AP+ML} Guidelines do not differentiate by patient and subgroup studies give no general decision rule; electronic medical records are large and longitudinal but not randomized; enter by recommending a regimen at each visit that beats the standard of care on HbA1c (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Per visit, predict post-treatment HbA1c for each regimen on an incremental menu by kNN with distance weights from per-regimen regression coefficients and k_t = 0.34 sqrt(n_t); prescribe the best only if it beats the current regimen by delta = 0.8%; impute counterfactuals by the same weighted matching on held-out visits; dashboard with provider override (pp. 2-7).
assumptions: 10,806 patients and 48,140 visits (1999-2014); lines of therapy cut at regimen changes or 500-day gaps; visits every 100 days; outcome = mean HbA1c 75-200 days later; standard of care = regimen given; lower HbA1c always better, single outcome, no individualized targets or adverse events, no socio-economic factors, GLP-1 agonists not separate, BMC population, unfilled prescriptions possible (pp. 2-3, 7).
proof_devices: No optimization model: argmin over a small incremental menu with a switching threshold delta (pp. 3-4)
Supervised kNN distance weights from per-treatment OLS coefficient magnitudes (p. 4)
Square-root rule for k fitted from RMSE-optimal values, k_t = 0.34 sqrt(n_t) (p. 5)
Counterfactual imputation by weighted matching on test-set neighbours, citing Imbens and Rubin (p. 5)
experiments: R 3.3.0; prediction R2 0.20-0.54 (kNN), 0.24-0.53 (LASSO, random forests); delta tuned on 'a single test set'; all visits: HbA1c 0.14% lower than standard of care (SE 0.01, P < 0.001); 15,323 visits (31.8%) where the algorithm differs: 0.44 +/- 0.03% lower (8.37% -> 7.93%), median 0.21%; LASSO and forest variants 0.13% and 0.07%; subgroups 0.05-0.22%; three other random splits 0.11-0.15%; the 48,140 visits called 'the test set' in the abstract are all visits in the data set; evaluator shares the predictor's matching structure; no run times (pp. 1, 3-7).
positioning: Against guideline algorithms, the ADA-EASD patient-centred statement and single-subgroup studies; within machine learning in health care and causal inference (Rosenbaum-Rubin, Imbens-Rubin); claims the first prescriptive method for personalized type 2 diabetes care; no OR literature beyond the authors' own (pp. 1-2, 5, 7-8).
writing: Clinical-journal format; effects in % and mmol/mol; 'novel' four times and 'novelty' once; abstract headline on the disagreement subset (-0.44%) beside the 68.2% agreement rate, the all-visit -0.14% only in Results and Table 2; specific listed limits; kNN interpretability argued (pp. 1-7).
limits_future: Stated: non-randomized data, counterfactuals only estimated, missing socio-economic factors and preferences, GLP-1 not separate, representativeness, adherence unknown, single outcome, no individualized targets; future: other hospitals, a clinical trial, genomic data (p. 7).

method_links.note: decision = regimen per visit, owner = provider, baseline = standard of care actually given, scored by the outcome under the decision rather than prediction R2, provider override, clinical trial named as next step; reports retrospective records only, so it cannot settle the diabetes-trial outcomes the skill lists as unverified
no optimization model; prediction and choice in two steps; threshold tuned on a test set; the evaluator shares the predictor's matching structure
delta as a single knob trading the number of switches against mean benefit among switchers, described in words; no curve published

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: agreement rate with practice (68.2%) reported with the effect on the visits where the algorithm departs from practice (-0.44%), the all-visit mean (-0.14%) and medians

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Counterfactual replay against the historical decision-maker
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: outcomes of the recommended regimen imputed by weighted matching on held-out visits and compared with the observed standard-of-care outcome; see S078 and S143

transferable: Define decision epochs and outcome windows from the clinical process and biology (lines of therapy, a visit every 100 days, the outcome 75-200 days later) so each record is one decision with one outcome (pp. 2-3).
Weight a kNN distance by per-treatment regression coefficients so neighbours are close on what predicts the outcome, and scale k with sqrt(n) per treatment (pp. 4-5).

Recommend a change only when the predicted gain clears a threshold, which keeps most decisions at the status quo and concentrates changes where the gain is large (pp. 4, 6); tune the threshold on validation data, not on the evaluation set.
Report together the agreement rate with practice, the effect on the cases of disagreement, the all-case mean and median, and subgroup effects (pp. 5-6).
Ship the recommendation with its evidence: the outcome distribution of the nearest neighbours under each option, and a provider override (pp. 6-7).
coauthors: Nathan Kallus, Alexander M. Weinstein, Ying Daisy Zhuo

quotes.text: guidelines for managing type 2 diabetes do not differentiate based on patient-specific factors
we can only estimate counterfactual outcomes
